strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: adapting LoRA adapters to heterogeneous quantization configurations for edge deployment, avoiding per-configuration fine-tuning.

The design is sensible and grounded in observation: the analysis (Appendix C.1) showing adaptation signal concentrates in L2 motivates the lightweight r×r adjustment Uθ(Ci) rather than predicting the full LoRA parameters, which keeps the configuration-aware model tractable.

The cyclic training procedure combining Gaussian-process/EHVI-based configuration search with diversity-preserving Pareto filtering is technically coherent and the algorithm is clearly described (Algorithm 1).

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation: four GLUE tasks, three LLM backbones (1.5B–7B) on C4, HV metrics across 50 configurations, unseen-configuration generalization tests, ablations on configuration search, rank sensitivity, and the number of Pareto segments U.

The reported results (better HV than per-configuration baselines at comparable or lower total training time; strong generalization to unseen configurations) support the central claim of efficient multi-configuration adaptation.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is largely a combination of known components—hypernetwork-style configuration conditioning, the L2-reparameterization of LoRA (Zhu et al., 2024), and standard multi-objective Bayesian optimization (EHVI) with a finite-difference/coordinate-search wrapper. Each ingredient is incremental, and the integration, while useful, is not a fundamentally new technique.

Key methodological details are underspecified or unclear: (i) the finite-difference 'gradient' (Eq. 7) is computed w.r.t. learned layer-embedding coordinates Ci, but the actual update (Eq. 8) then shifts these embeddings by ±δ=1 in an apparently discrete configuration space—it is unclear how the embedding perturbation maps back to a valid discrete quantization configuration, and this is central to the method's validity; (ii) f1 is evaluated on a single calibration batch, which introduces substantial evaluation noise into the GP surrogate, yet no variance handling or repeated evaluation is discussed.

The comparison methodology raises fairness concerns: CoA-LoRA is trained jointly across ~50 configurations, while baselines are fine-tuned per configuration; nevertheless Table 2 reports CoA-LoRA as faster overall (e.g., 57m vs 79m on QNLI), which is counterintuitive given CoA-LoRA's additional GP/finite-difference evaluation overhead, and the accounting of what 'training time' includes is not explained.

The hypervolume evaluation protocol (Eq. 13 normalization, choice of reference point (1,1)) is unusual and can materially affect the reported HV numbers; accuracy-gap figures are also confusing (e.g., Table 2 reports Shared-LoRA MNLI gap as +8.93% while the text cites it as evidence of degraded accuracy; Table 3 shows negative gaps for CoA-LoRA in some rank settings, weakening the 'consistent superiority' claim). No statistical significance, error bars, or multiple seeds are reported.

Scope of evaluation is somewhat narrow for a top-tier venue: GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-Large (rather than instruction/LLM fine-tuning benchmarks such as Alpaca/LIMA) and C4 perplexity; results on LLMs are confined to perplexity and a small zero-shot appendix table with small margins over baselines.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the abstract's 'gains of 2.36% to 10.37%' cherry-picks the best per-task gaps relative to Q-LoRA only, whereas LQ-LoRA (the stronger baseline) is closer or occasionally ahead at some ranks; the generalization claim on SST-2 is explained post hoc rather than analyzed.

No code or reproducibility plan is mentioned; given the many hyperparameters (T1, T2, U, δ, GP kernel choices, 50 initial configurations, Gurobi-based initialization), independent reproduction would be difficult.

Presentation issues: several equations and definitions are loosely stated (e.g., Eq. 11's storage constraint notation, the role of layer-name and block-index embeddings m and b is mentioned but their learned form is never defined), and Figure 1's motivating experiment is limited to a single task/model.

strengths: The problem addressed is practical and well-motivated: supporting many quantization configurations from a single trained model avoids the linear cost blow-up of per-configuration LoRA fine-tuning, which is a real deployment concern for heterogeneous edge devices.

The core design idea is sensible: exploiting the empirical observation (supported by Appendix C.1 correlation analysis) that most configuration-specific adaptation signal resides in L2 allows a lightweight r×r configuration-aware adjustment instead of predicting full LoRA parameters, keeping the hypernetwork tractable.

The two-component method (configuration-aware adjustment + Pareto/GP-based configuration set search) is coherently integrated in a cyclic training procedure, and Algorithm 1 plus the appendix (initial configuration construction via SVD-guided 0-1 optimization with Gurobi) provide a reasonably complete description of the pipeline.

The empirical evaluation covers multiple axes: four GLUE tasks, language modeling on C4 with three LLMs (1.5B–7B), hypervolume comparisons, total training time, generalization to unseen configurations (Fig. 7), sensitivity to rank (Table 3), segment count U, and zero-shot transfer on eight tasks (Table C.3).
Ablations (Fig. 8 for configuration search; Fig. C.2 for Pareto filtering) directly probe the two main proposed components rather than only reporting the full system.
weaknesses: Technical soundness of the configuration search is under-specified and somewhat dubious: the Gaussian process is defined over discrete, high-dimensional configuration embeddings (Eq. 5, with an RBF kernel over configurations?), yet finite-difference 'gradients' (Eq. 7) are taken w.r.t. continuous layer-embedding coordinates and then turned into ±1 discrete moves via Eq. 8. The relationship between the continuous surrogate and the discrete search space is never clarified, and no theoretical or empirical justification is given that this EHVI-based coordinate search is better than simpler discrete search strategies (e.g., random perturbation, evolutionary search).

Internal inconsistency in the evaluation metric: Section 4.3 and Fig. 4 state that a larger hypervolume indicates a better Pareto front, but Appendix B Eq. (13) and Table C.2 describe a normalization after which 'smaller values indicate better performance.' The sign conventions of the reported 'Gap' columns are also confusing and inconsistent between Table 2 (positive gap = better than Q-LoRA) and Table C.2 (positive perplexity gap = good, negative = bad, with 'average decrease in perplexity (lower is better)' in the caption). This undermines confidence in the headline numbers.

Missing relevant baselines and positioning: methods supporting multiple/variable bit-widths from a single model, most notably Any-Precision LLM and other nested/elastic-quantization approaches, are neither discussed nor compared. Since the paper's central claim is serving arbitrary configurations without re-fine-tuning, comparison against variable-precision inference methods is essential and its absence weakens the significance claims.

The edge-device motivation is asserted but never tested: there are no measurements of on-device memory footprint, dequantization overhead of NF quantization, or inference latency at any configuration; the evaluation is entirely offline fine-tuning accuracy/perplexity on server-scale hardware. The practicality story remains unverified.

Cost accounting for the headline efficiency claim ('no additional time cost') is incomplete. Table 2 reports only the training time of the configuration-aware model; the overhead of evaluating candidate configurations on calibration data, fitting the GP, and running the EHVI coordinate search each epoch (over 50 configurations, each requiring quantized forward passes) is not itemized. The comparison of 57m (CoA-LoRA) vs. 79m (Q-LoRA for 4 configurations) may thus be less favorable than presented.

Attribution of gains is unclear. Because CoA-LoRA effectively trains on many configurations jointly, part of the improvement over Q-LoRA may come from any multi-configuration regularization effect rather than the proposed mapping or search. A control experiment (e.g., a shared LoRA trained across the searched configuration set without the configuration-aware model, or the hypernetwork with a randomly sampled configuration set of equal size) is needed to isolate the contribution; Shared-LoRA does not fully serve this role.

Several results are mixed or fragile: accuracy gaps relative to Q-LoRA are negative in several rank/task cells of Table 3 (e.g., MNLI r=64, r=128), U=40 hurts SST-2, and Fig. 8 shows the configuration-search component contributes little on MNLI/QQP. The narrative of 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art' overstates what the evidence supports.

No code or reproducibility artifact is mentioned. Given the many interacting components (Gurobi initialization, GP surrogate, EHVI finite-difference search, segmented Pareto filtering with U=40), independent reproduction without source code appears difficult.

Writing and presentation issues: typos ('ANLL' for ANLI, grammar errors), the solution-count column of Table 2 ('4' vs '1' vs '∞') is unexplained, and several tables require cross-referencing the appendix to interpret, which hurts clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: serving quantized LLMs across heterogeneous bit-width budgets without repeatedly fine-tuning a separate LoRA adapter per configuration. The motivation (Fig. 1) clearly illustrates the accuracy/time trade-off between one-to-one fine-tuning (Q-LoRA) and a single shared adapter.

The technical approach is reasonable: restricting the configuration-aware model's output to a small r x r adjustment on L2 (motivated by an empirical analysis in Appendix C.1 showing L2 carries shared information) makes the mapping tractable, and the cyclic procedure combining model training with Pareto/GP-based configuration search is coherent.

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive: two settings (GLUE with RoBERTa-Large and C4 perplexity with Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B and Llama-2-7B), multiple ranks (32/64/128), comparisons across seen/unseen configurations (Fig. 7), zero-shot downstream evaluation (Table C.3), and ablations on the configuration search (Fig. 8) and the number of Pareto segments (Fig. C.2).

The hypervolume-based evaluation over the accuracy-vs-bit-width trade-off is an appropriate and well-formalized way to compare methods that operate across many configurations, and the appendix documents reference points and normalization.

Reproducibility details are relatively thorough: configuration space (Table 1), initial configuration generation via a 0-1 integer program (Appendix A.1), training settings, adjustable layers, and the full algorithm pseudocode are provided.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. The method is essentially a small hypernetwork that emits per-layer low-rank adjustments conditioned on quantization settings, combined with standard Bayesian optimization machinery (GP surrogate, EHVI acquisition, hypervolume filtering). Each component is well known; the contribution is the composition, and the paper could better contrast against related hypernetwork/once-for-all and mixed-precision NAS-style approaches.

The core finite-difference optimization (Eqs. 7-8) is technically under-specified and conceptually questionable: the configuration space is discrete, yet the method perturbs 'the i-th layer embedding' by unit steps in a learned embedding space and takes a sign of an approximate gradient of the EHVI. It is unclear how an update in embedding space maps back to a valid discrete configuration (bit-widths, bucket sizes), and no analysis of this search's convergence or cost is given.

Baseline comparisons are asymmetric: CoA-LoRA is evaluated over 50 configurations spanning 2.5-6.25 bits, while Q-LoRA/LQ-LoRA are only evaluated at 2.5, 3, 3.5, and 4 bits. HV values are therefore computed over partially overlapping bit-width ranges, and extrapolating baselines to low bit-widths via figures is not a rigorous comparison.

Efficiency claims are overstated relative to the reported numbers: CoA-LoRA takes 57-91 minutes vs. 61-132 minutes for LQ-LoRA (Table 2) in the one-to-one comparison shown; the claimed savings rely on baselines needing one run per additional configuration, but the task-specific training cost of the configuration-aware model itself is substantial, and the framework is not task-agnostic (a separate CoA-LoRA model appears needed per task/dataset).

No variance reporting: results are single runs without error bars or seeds, which is a concern given that 'accuracy gaps' as large as 10.37% are highlighted as headline contributions and some gaps change sign across ranks (e.g., -0.63% at r=64 MNLI vs. +9.60% at r=32).

Some inconsistencies and gaps in presentation: the appendix states smaller HV values indicate better performance while the main text says larger HV is better; Fig. 5 y-axis scales and curve overlaps make per-bit-width comparisons hard to verify; and the claim of generalization to 'arbitrary' configurations is only tested for configurations with similar average bit-widths.

Evaluation uses weight-only NF quantization and relatively small models (up to 7B) on C4 perplexity and GLUE; there is no evaluation of inference-time cost of the configuration-aware model on-device, which is central to the motivating edge-deployment scenario.

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: adapting LoRA fine-tuning of quantized LLMs to arbitrary quantization configurations for heterogeneous edge devices, avoiding the prohibitive cost of per-configuration fine-tuning.

The core technical idea is sensible: a lightweight per-layer mapping (configuration embedding -> r x r adjustment applied as (I+U)L2) drastically reduces output dimensionality compared to generating full LoRA parameters, and is supported by an empirical observation (Appendix C.1) that configuration-specific signal concentrates in L2.

The Pareto/GP-based configuration set search with hypervolume improvement and diversity-preserving segmented Pareto filtering is a thoughtful treatment of the nontrivial problem of selecting training configurations.

Comprehensive experiments: GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-Large, perplexity on C4 for Qwen-2.5-1.5B/3B and LLaMA-2-7B/13B, multiple ranks (32/64/128), integer mixed-precision quantization, zero-shot downstream evaluation, generalization to unseen configurations (Fig. 7), and ablations on configuration search and the number of segments U.

Strong efficiency story: a single ~1 hour training serves all configurations, versus 20-40 minutes per configuration for QLoRA/LQ-LoRA, with competitive or better accuracy (Table 2, Table C.2, Table C.4).

Reproducibility support is reasonable: architecture details, initial configuration generation via integer programming (with solver and timing), reference points for HV, and algorithm pseudocode are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Methodological soundness of the configuration search is ad hoc: finite-difference gradients of EHVI over a continuous embedding of a discrete configuration space with step size delta=1 is a heuristic with no convergence or validity analysis; the coordinate-wise sign update (Eq. 8) may oscillate on discrete choices, and no comparison against simpler discrete multi-objective optimizers (e.g., NSGA-II, random search with Pareto filtering beyond 'random extension') is provided.

Some evaluation fairness concerns: CoA-LoRA is evaluated over 50 configurations while QLoRA/LQ-LoRA are only run at 5 bit-widths, which may bias the hypervolume comparison in CoA-LoRA's favor; the layer-wise automatic configuration for baselines (Eq. 11) differs from their native setups (e.g., uniform-bit QLoRA), making 'gap relative to QLoRA' hard to interpret.

Scale of the most rigorous quantitative comparisons is limited: the accuracy-gap and time results (Table 2) are on RoBERTa-Large rather than an actual LLM; LLM experiments rely mainly on C4 perplexity, which is a weaker proxy for real deployment quality than instruction tuning or task-level evaluation at LLM scale.

Inconsistencies and clarity issues: Eq. 11 appears to add L1|X + L2|X rather than the product L1L2 used elsewhere; the 'Solution' column in Table 2 is not explained; Fig. C.3 labels the segment count as K while the text uses U; the sentence 'Our implementation is available at' is truncated. The claimed 'no additional time cost' is imprecise since CoA-LoRA takes ~2x the time of Shared-LoRA.

No experimental comparison with the closest related methods discussed in Section 2.3 (LoRA-Gen, ICM-LoRA, CONP-DIFF), even in a variant form, leaving the positioning against conditional LoRA-generation approaches unvalidated.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters is acknowledged but not resolved: U=40 is worse than U=20 on SST-2, and the post-hoc explanations (task simplicity) are speculative; no principled guidance for choosing U, T, delta, or calibration batch size.

The claim that 'most of the adaptation signal is concentrated in L2' rests on correlation analyses of similarity matrices; this does not establish that transforming only L2 can fully recover configuration-specific adaptation, and no ablation of adjusting L1 instead is reported.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: adapting a single LoRA adapter to arbitrary (mixed-precision) quantization configurations, avoiding costly per-configuration fine-tuning. This is a genuine pain point for serving quantized LLMs across heterogeneous devices.

The overall design is reasonable and clearly motivated: a lightweight hypernetwork that produces per-layer r×r adjustments conditioned on layer-level quantization configurations, plus a Pareto/GP-based search over the training configuration set. Decomposing the output space layer-wise is a sensible way to tame dimensionality.

The experimental coverage is fairly broad: GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-Large, C4 perplexity on Qwen-2.5-1.5B/3B, LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B, multiple ranks (32/64/128), integer mixed-precision quantization, zero-shot evaluation on eight downstream tasks, and several ablations (configuration search, number of segments U, seen vs. unseen configurations).

Ablations support the claimed contributions: the guided Pareto search outperforms frozen and randomly extended configuration sets, and the seen/unseen comparison (Fig. 7) provides some evidence of generalization to configurations not observed during training.

The appendix contains sufficient algorithmic and implementation detail (mapper architecture, configuration initialization via integer programming, HV normalization) that the method is largely reproducible in principle.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core mechanism—a conditional hypernetwork generating LoRA adjustments—is a straightforward extension of existing adapter-generation work (CONDP-DIFF, ICM-LoRA, LoRA-Gen), and the configuration search is essentially standard Bayesian optimization with EHVI plus a finite-difference/coordinate-descent heuristic (Eq. 7–8) applied to a discrete space without theoretical justification. The combination is competent but incremental.

Missing key related baselines. The 'one model serving many bit-widths' setting has directly relevant prior work (e.g., Any-Precision LLM / nested or elastic quantization, one-for-all compression) that is not discussed or compared. The chosen baselines (QLoRA, LQ-LoRA, GPTQ-LoRA, Shared-LoRA) make the proposed comparison favorable but incomplete.

The edge-deployment motivation is asserted but never validated. The motivating experiment (Fig. 1) uses only RoBERTa-Large on SST-2; the largest models evaluated (up to 13B) are not edge devices, and there are no measurements of latency, memory, or adapter switching cost on actual hardware. The practical benefit over simply shipping a few pre-tuned adapters is not quantified.

Fairness and clarity concerns in the comparison protocol. Baselines are evaluated at 5–6 bit-widths while CoA-LoRA is evaluated over 50 configurations, and the 'accuracy gap' is computed relative to QLoRA over only four bit-widths, which can bias the HV and gap summaries. The reported training-time comparison (CoA-LoRA training a hypernetwork over ~50 configurations in less wall-clock time than QLoRA fine-tunes a handful of configurations) deserves closer scrutiny and clearer accounting of the search/evaluation overhead.

There is an apparent inconsistency in the method's motivation: the paper claims configuration-specific knowledge resides primarily in L1 (Appendix C.1), yet the configuration-aware model modulates L2 via (I + U_theta)L2 (Eq. 2). The rationale for conditioning on L2 is not well reconciled with this empirical observation.

Overstated claims. 'Adapts to arbitrary quantization configurations' is not supported: the configuration space is restricted to the NF parameterization in Table 1, training configurations span only 2.25–7.25 bits, and generalization is tested only within this range with similar average bit-widths. Extrapolation and robustness to out-of-distribution configurations are untested.

Presentation issues undermine polish: an incomplete sentence ('Our implementation is available a', Sec. 5.1), duplicated text in Appendix A.1 ('The output is reshaped into an r×r adjustment matrix' appears twice), inconsistent notation (U vs. K for segments in Appendix C.3), confusing gap signs in Tables 2/3, and GP fitting on f1 evaluated with a single batch of calibration data, which makes the surrogate noisy.

Significance is moderate: the gains, while consistent, are modest for GLUE tasks at higher bit-widths, and perplexity results (Table C.5) show CoA-LoRA sometimes loses to QLoRA; the headline '1.74%–8.89% gains' aggregates across configurations in a way that is hard to verify from the reported tables.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: adapting a single LoRA adapter to arbitrary quantization configurations for heterogeneous edge devices, avoiding repeated per-configuration fine-tuning.

The design is well-motivated by an empirical observation (adaptation signal concentrated in L2 matrices, Appendix C.1), and the lightweight r×r adjustment is an elegant way to reduce the output dimensionality of the hypernetwork.

The Pareto-based configuration search with hypervolume/EHVI and diversity-preserving segmentation is a thoughtful addition; the ablation (Fig. 8) convincingly shows that guided configuration search outperforms both a frozen set and random extension.

Experiments are fairly comprehensive: four GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-Large, C4 fine-tuning on Qwen-2.5 (1.5B/3B), LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B, multiple ranks (32/64/128), integer mixed-precision quantization, zero-shot evaluation on seven downstream tasks, and generalization analysis on unseen configurations.

Efficiency claims are supported: a single ~1-hour training run serves all configurations versus 20–40 minutes per configuration for QLoRA/LQ-LoRA, which is a meaningful practical advantage at deployment time.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: implementation is stated to be available, and appendices provide architecture details, hyperparameters, the ILP formulation for initial configuration generation, and reference points for HV computation.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. Hypernetwork/conditional LoRA generation is well established (LoRA-Gen, ICM-LoRA, CONDP-DIFF, G.pt), and the 'once-for-all' idea of serving many compression configurations from one trained model is standard in mixed-precision NAS (e.g., once-for-all networks, slimmable networks), which the related work does not discuss or position against. The main novelty is applying this to quantization configurations plus the Pareto search, which is incremental.

Evaluation fairness concerns: CoA-LoRA is evaluated over 50 configurations (2.5–6.25 bits) while baselines are only fine-tuned at 5 bit-widths. The hypervolume comparison in Table 2/C.2 may therefore be structurally biased toward CoA-LoRA, since a broader coverage range mechanically inflates HV; an HV comparison at matched bit-width points would be more convincing.

Reported gains are not uniformly positive in the appendix: QLoRA beats CoA-LoRA on most LLaMA-2-13B bit settings (Table C.4), several LLaMA-2-7B rank/bit cells favor baselines (Table C.5), and zero-shot results are mixed (Shared-LoRA wins on Llama-2-7B average). The main-text claim of 'consistently outperforming' methods is stronger than the full evidence warrants.

The finite-difference gradient approximation of EHVI over a discrete configuration space (Eq. 7–8, δ=1) is technically ad hoc. It is unclear what δ means for discrete layer-level configuration variables, how the embedding-space perturbation maps back to valid discrete configurations, and why coordinate-wise sign updates are effective; a theoretical or empirical justification is missing.

No variance reporting: results appear to come from single runs without error bars, seeds, or significance tests, despite known instability of LoRA fine-tuning (which the authors themselves use to criticize Shared-LoRA).

Several clarity issues: the 'Solution = ∞' column in Table 2 is confusing and unexplained; Eq. (2) notation (L1·(I+U)L2 vs. the stated (I+U)L2) is inconsistent; typos such as 'probilitively high-dimensional' recur; and the motivation figure (Fig. 1) has illegible axis labels.

Task scope is somewhat narrow for the deployment story: detailed accuracy comparisons are confined to GLUE classification with RoBERTa-Large and C4 perplexity; no instruction-following or generative task benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K) at LLM scale, which would better substantiate the edge-deployment motivation.
